analytic.title: Work-in-Progress: Generalized Demand-Based Schedulability Test for Dual-Criticality Sporadic Task Model

div.p: In this paper, we consider the scheduling of dualcriticality sporadic task systems with arbitrary deadlines using demand bound functions. In dual-criticality systems, tasks are assigned either low-criticality or high-criticality based on assurance needs with associated worst-case execution times. Arbitrary deadlines are those that allow the deadline to be larger than the minimum separation between consecutive task instances. Demand bound functions have been used to successfully schedule dualcriticality task sets for constrained deadlines, i.e., deadlines that are always less than or equal to minimum inter-arrival separation time. We formulate a new demand bound function for a more generalized dual-criticality task system with both constrained and arbitrary deadlines on a preemptive uniprocessor.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Scheduling sporadic tasks has proved to be a challenge since no a priori knowledge of their arrival times exists. The minimum separation time between two consecutive releases of jobs or instances of the same task provides some level of predictability. However, sporadic tasks can produce an infinite number of jobs, with the next set of jobs often different from the current one [4]. This challenge is exacerbated in a mixed-criticality setting in which each task has a criticality level assigned to it. Different levels of assurance assume tasks will execute for a varying amount of time depending on their criticality levels. In order to be schedulable on a uniprocessor, each task has to meet its deadline based on the current system's criticality mode and corresponding execution times.

Mixed-criticality systems reflect the trend of combining functionalities of different importance on the same platform [2]. These systems are gaining popularity especially in the automotive and aerospace industries [4]. Integrating multiple functions produces less complex and more cost-effective systems [5]. However, these functionalities require different levels of assurance, and determining an adequate worst-case execution time (WCET) of each task in such a system to accommodate these needs often leads to pessimistic estimates.

For example, a certification authority and a system designer have opposing and incompatible goals when it comes to finding a WCET [4]. A system designer cares about the *Supported in part by a UH Provost Global Faculty Funds Award. efficient usage of limited resources and favors a smaller, less pessimistic WCET [4]. Representatives from agencies like the Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) or the European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) prioritize consumer safety and use a more pessimistic method to calculate a larger WCET [4].

Mixed-criticality models offer a solution to opposing assurance needs. A list of WCETs, one for each criticality level, accommodates different needs and gives a higher level of assurance that the actual execution time would not surpass the WCET [6]. Differentiating levels of assurance and using different estimates for WCET satisfy the needs of both the system designer and the certification authority.

A dual-criticality system has a low-criticality mode that indicates normal operating conditions, and a high-criticality mode that indicates a deviation from normal conditions [1]. A deviation from normal occurs when a task executes for more than its least pessimistic (smallest) WCET. Tasks with a lowcriticality level would be discarded once the system enters high-criticality mode. The system recognizes this deviation and requires only high-criticality tasks to meet their deadlines.

Existing work on mixed-criticality sporadic tasks has limited task deadlines. Some assume implicit deadlines, i.e., deadlines equal minimum separation times [4], [9]. Others use constrained deadlines, i.e., deadlines less than or equal to minimum separation times [1], [2], [6], [8]. However, it is important to consider arbitrary deadlines, i.e., deadlines that can be greater than their minimum separation time [3]. In signal processing, for example, buffers can postpone processing to come after the sampling period [3]. More generally, systems that have sufficiently large buffers will allow tasks to respond past their period as long as buffers have enough storage [7].

Arbitrary deadlines have not been adequately addressed in the mixed-criticality setting. Vestal [6] initiated the conversation on mixed-criticality scheduling by adjusting Audsley's priority assignment algorithm. Vestal's [6] algorithm assumed constrained deadlines, as did Baruah's [8] work that developed upon Vestal's with an improved Adaptive Mixed Criticality priority assignment scheme. Baruah [4] also proposed EDF-VD for scheduling task sets with implicit deadlines that implemented a utilization-based schedulability test.

More Earliest Deadline First (EDF) schedulers for mixedcriticality systems emerged. Ekberg and Yi [2] proposed the first demand bound functions to determine schedulability for a mixed-criticality task model. Easwaran [1] improved upon this idea and demonstrated significantly better performance with a new deadline tightening strategy, Earliest Carry-over Deadline First. Both papers assumed constrained deadlines [1], [2].

Few papers deal with unconstrained deadlines, but only in cases that assume the criticality level of each job is determined by the job itself. Guan et al. [10] proposed a fixed-priority, polynomial-time scheduler: Priority List Reuse Scheduling. The criticality level is exhibited by the job when it signals completion [10] instead of being specified by the system [6]. With no switch between two system modes, this algorithm cannot be directly applied with trivial modifications.

Burns and Davis [7] expanded fixed priority assignment scheduling in Adaptive Mixed Criticality (AMC) setting for arbitrary deadlines and semi-clairvoyant tasks. Their work builds upon Agrawal's [9] introduction of semi-clairvoyance in mixed-criticality models for a fixed number of jobs with implicit deadlines. The semi-clairvoyant tasks in Burns and Davis' [7] AMC model announce upon arrival if the task will exceed the smallest WCET. Neither [7] nor [10] considers cases in which the whole system switches into another mode, requiring jobs to adapt to behavior change during execution.

We propose new demand bound functions for dual-criticality sporadic task models with unconstrained deadlines to test EDF schedulability on a unit-speed processor. In our model, the system indicates the switch between modes. The switch in modes causes execution demand to change based on the criticality level of the task, making it difficult to predict. We not only bound the demand of jobs in low-and high-criticality mode, but also find the maximum possible demand for jobs that are released before the switch with deadlines after it.

div.head: A. Notation
div.p: For consistency, we use notations similar or identical to those in [1], [2]. To represent dual-criticality, we use LO as an abbreviation for low-criticality and HI for high-criticality.

Each dual-criticality sporadic task τ i can be defined as a tuple of four parameters (T i , D i , L i , C i ). T i denotes the minimum separation interval between two consecutive releases of the task's jobs or instances. D i denotes the relative deadline. D i can be greater, equal to, or less than T i . Note that with unconstrained deadlines, there can be more than one job active for the same task at the same time. L i indicates the level of criticality where L i ∈ {LO, HI}. C i is a list of worst-case execution times, {C LO i , C HI i }, where C LO i corresponds to a less pessimistic WCET and C HI i to a more pessimistic WCET. For models with more than two criticality levels, there needs to be a WCET corresponding to each criticality level. We assume discrete time, so parameters T i and D i are positive integers, and C i is a list of positive integers.

We denote a set of sporadic tasks as τ = {τ 1 , ..., τ n }. Each job of task τ i with 1 ≤ i ≤ n will be released with minimum inter-arrival separation of T i time units and have a deadline at D i time units after its release. In addition, we let L(τ ) be the set of LO tasks in τ and H(τ ) be the set of HI tasks in τ .

div.head: B. System Requirements and Assumptions
div.p: For simplicity, we consider a system that switches at the task level, i.e., a running task that exceeds its C LO i triggers the switch to high-criticality mode. Our ongoing work investigates system level switches, in which a mode switch occurs when the workload exceeds the maximum threshold for a given period.

Before the switch, the system runs in low-criticality mode and operating conditions are assumed to be normal. In this mode, both LO and HI criticality tasks execute within C LO i and are expected to meet their deadlines. The switch indicates that the system has deviated from its normal mode. We assume LO tasks are discarded and only HI tasks are required to meet their deadlines. In addition, HI tasks will be expected to execute until C HI i , increasing their demand on the processor. div.head: C. Adjusting Relative Deadlines
div.p: The switch to high-criticality mode allows HI tasks to execute until their largest WCET, raising the demand on the processor. Tightening HI tasks' deadlines in advance while the system is in low-criticality mode will allow for some slack in high-criticality mode, although at the cost of increased demand in low-criticality mode [2]. Finding an appropriate tightened deadline for HI tasks will use the discrepancy between C LO i and C HI i to balance execution demand in both modes to make the trade-off worthwhile. Moving the deadline earlier than its original value does not violate the deadline satisfaction. We let Di be the tightened deadline, and assume Di = D i for LO tasks and Di ≤ D i for HI tasks.

div.head: D. Carry-Over Jobs
div.p: In a mixed-criticality setting, it is important to account for the possibility of jobs that were released or running at the time of each switch. These jobs are called carry-over jobs.

Definition 1: A task's job that was released in one mode and has a deadline in another mode is known as a carry-over job. Let t CO be the release time of a carry-over job of task τ i and t s be the time of the mode switch. Then t CO ≤ t s and t s < t CO + D i , or equivalently, t s + 1 ≤ t CO + D i .
Next, Easwaran [1] introduced a type of carry-over job called unnecessary job. Although this type of job will be discarded at the time of a switch, it still contributes to demand.

Definition 2: A task's job that was released in one mode and has a deadline in another mode higher than its own criticality level is known as an unnecessary job. This type of carry-over jobs will be discarded at the time of the mode switch.

div.head: E. A Demand Bound Function for Sporadic Tasks
div.p: A demand bound function (dbf) gives the maximum demand on a processor for a given task τ i and time interval t such that the job's deadline D i falls within t. The number of such jobs of τ i can be characterized by a non-negative k + 1 such that k is the largest number satisfying k
Proposition 1: A demand bound function dbf (τ i , t) returns the maximum execution demand of task τ i with deadlines in the given period t [3]. The dbf for τ i with parameters
div.formula: (T i , D i , C i ) is: dbf (τ i , t) = C i • max 0, t -D i T i + 1
div.p: The dbf returns the same maximum demand given any time period of the same length. Also, the function does not assume that the deadline is less than or equal to minimum separation, allowing us to use it with unconstrained deadlines, i.e., tasks with D i > T i . Baruah et al. [3] proposed a necessary and sufficient condition for scheduling a general (non-mixedcriticality) sporadic task set using demand bound functions.
Proposition 2: A task set is feasibly schedulable (Theorem 1 in [3]) by EDF algorithm on a unit-speed uniprocessor iff τi∈τ dbf (τ i , t) ≤ t, ∀0 ≤ t ≤ t M AX , where
div.formula: t M AX = min{T + max 1≤i≤n {D i }, U 1 -U • max 1≤i≤n {T i -D i }},
div.p: where
div.formula: T = lcm 1≤i≤n {T i } and U = n i=1 C i T i
div.p: If Proposition 2 holds for these conditions, then it will hold true for all t > t M AX as long as the utilization of the task set U = n i=1 Ci Ti ≤ 1 [3]. t M AX can be calculated in pseudopolynomial time [3].

div.head: F. Existing Demand Bound Functions for Mixed-Criticalities
div.p: Previous work on dual-criticality sporadic task systems have formulated their demand bound functions based on how carryover jobs affect demand. These dbf's and their schedulability tests were made for constrained deadlines, i.e., D i ≤ T i . Ekberg and Yi [2] assumed all deadlines would be met in lowcriticality mode to derive separate functions for each criticality mode. For high-criticality mode, they [2] derived the difference between real and tightened deadlines to derive bounds for the remaining scheduling window of a carry-over job. Easwaran [1] improved these dbf's by tying low and high demand bound functions together. He divided tasks into mutually exclusive cases based on their criticality level and potential to be a carryover task. His dbf was tighter than the previous one.

div.head: III. FORMULATING A NEW DEMAND BOUND FUNCTION
div.p: In this section, we demonstrate our approach to formulating a new demand-based schedulability test with unconstrained deadlines. Since dbf's in Proposition 1 and 2 by Baruah et al. [3] do not assume constrained deadlines, we can expand on them for our dual-criticality model. Our proposed dbf's take into account the potential for carry-over or unnecessary jobs. Let t s be the time of the mode switch. If t s ≥ t or t s = 0, the system would stay in a single mode for its entire execution and Proposition 1 would apply. It would be simple to extend Proposition 2 to accommodate the different parameters for these trivial cases. Thus, in the discussion below, we assume 0 < t s < t. Under this assumption, we can divide the given period t into two intervals [0, t s ] and (t s , t]. By definition, the program will execute in low-criticality mode in [0, t s ] and high-criticality mode in (t s , t].

Jobs of tasks fall under four mutually exclusive cases based on the tasks' criticality level L i , release times t 0 , and relative deadlines D i . The first two cases are jobs that are released and have deadlines in the same mode, either low-or high-criticality mode. The latter two cases are jobs that are released in one mode and have deadlines in another, differentiated by their criticality levels. If we can formulate a dbf for each case, then the sum of those dbf's can give us a schedulability test using Proposition 2. The cases are as follows:
div.formula: • Case 1: τ i ∈ τ s.t. t 0 ∈ [0, t s ] and t 0 + Di ∈ [0, t s ] • Case 2: τ i ∈ H(τ ) s.t. t 0 ∈ (t s , t] and t 0 + D i ∈ (t s , t] • Case 3: τ i ∈ H(τ ) s.t. t 0 ∈ [0, t s ] and t 0 + Di ∈ (t s , t] • Case 4: τ i ∈ L(τ ) s.t. t 0 ∈ [0, t s ] and t 0 + Di ∈ (t s , t]
div.p: It is simple to extend Proposition 1 for Case 1 and 2, both for jobs of tasks with a release time and relative deadline in the same mode. We calculate the maximum demand given a period by multiplying the execution time C i by the number of job requests with deadlines in the same period. For Case 1, each task is expected to execute until C LO i and meet deadline Di , regardless of its criticality level L i . For Case 2, only HI tasks must run until C HI i and meet their original deadline D i . Case 3 and 4 deals with carry-over jobs and unnecessary jobs, i.e., jobs that will not have request times and deadlines in the same period by their definitions. We need to be able to determine the maximum number of requests in [0, t s ] with deadlines in (t s , t]. We do so with the following lemma, and Fig. 1 illustrates it further.

Lemma 1: During a given interval [a, b] of length b -a, a sporadic task τ i with minimum separation T i can have maximum max 0, b-a Ti + 1 number of requests. We can use Definition 1 and Lemma 1 to derive the maximum execution bound for Case 3. Let a job J i of task τ i ∈ H(τ ) with parameters (T i , Di , L i = HI, C HI i ) be a carry-over job. Let J i 's release time be denoted t CO . By Definition 1, t s -Di + 1 ≤ t CO ≤ t -Di . We know that the maximum number of requests by τ i in low-criticality mode is k LO = max 0, ts-Di Ti + 1 . Similarly, the maximum number of requests in high-criticality mode is k HI = max 0, t-ts-Di Ti + 1 . To maximize demand for carry-over jobs, we assume that jobs in lowcriticality mode were released as early as possible and jobs in high-criticality mode were released as late as possible. We find additional bounds for t CO by using the minimum separation time between jobs. The release time of the last job with a deadline before or at t s is (k LO -1) • T i . It follows that the earliest possible value for t CO is T i time units later at k LO •T i to satisfy the minimum separation constraint. This concept is demonstrated with Fig. 2(a). Similarly, the release time of the first job with a deadline before or at t is t-D i -(k HI -1)•T i . It follows that the latest possible value for t CO is T i time units earlier at t -D i -k HI • T i in order to satisfy the minimum separation constraint. This concept is shown in Fig. 2(b).

Lemma 1 applies the bounds derived above to get the maximum number of requests by a sporadic task within those bounds. Given a carry-over job's lower bound low CO and upper bound up CO , we get the maximum execution demand by multiplying C HI i by the maximum number of requests in the period [low CO , up CO ]. We apply a similar tactic to obtain a dbf for Case 4 dealing with unnecessary jobs. However, we do not have to satisfy the minimum separation constraint for the upper bound of an unnecessary job since these low-criticality jobs will be discarded after t s . We denote an unnecessary job's release time as t U N , its lower bound as low U N , and its upper bound as up U N . Applying Lemma 1 gets the maximum number of requests k by τ i in the period [low U N , up U N ]:
div.formula: k = max 0, up U N -low U N T i +1
div.p: In addition to bounding t U N , we keep in mind that all unnecessary jobs will stop executing at t s . To get the maximum demand, we assume that unnecessary jobs start executing when released. We determined that the earliest possible value for an unnecessary job's release time t U N is low U N , and each successive release is T i time units later. Then:
div.formula: t s -low U N + t s -low U N -T i + t s -low U N -2T i + • • • + t s -low U N +(k -1)T i = k •(t s -low U N )- k • (k -1) • T i2
div.p: Thus, the upper bound on demand is either k
div.formula: • C LO i or k • (t s -low U N ) -k•(k-1)•Ti 2
div.p: , whichever is smaller. As illustrated in the proof sketches above, we can use the properties of sporadic tasks and dual-criticality to derive a dbf for each case. The sum of the dbf's can give a sufficient condition for EDF schedulability by extending Proposition 2.

div.head: IV. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In this paper, we outline a method to formulate a demand bound function that can test the EDF schedulability of dualcriticality sporadic task sets with unconstrained deadlines. Our demand bound functions will bound the execution of not only tasks in low-or high-criticality mode, but also carryover tasks, i.e., tasks that were released or running when the mode switch happens. Our test make no assumptions about deadlines, whether implicit or constrained, differentiating it from previous work on dual-criticality models.

Our schedulability test, however, is a theoretical proposition at its current state. In the near future, we will elaborate on this model with detailed proofs and an experimental evaluation. We plan on comparing the performance of our schedulability test with those from previous research. In addition, we plan on developing a new deadline tightening algorithm for this test and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulations.
